904.title: leaving Vrindavan
904.howItsDone: Akrura's hymn in the Bhagavata is recited by devotees, and pilgrims bathe at a place on the Yamuna that tradition links with his vision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Vrindavan from the side of the ones who stay: the gopis in the road, a promise to come back, and the dust settling. Did you send that message to someone far away? Day nine hundred four.

On the road to Mathura, the chariot stops at the river. Akrura asks the boys to wait in the shade while he goes down to the Yamuna to bathe and say his prayers. He wades in, ducks under the water, and opens his eyes. Krishna and Balarama are there, under the river, looking at him. Which is strange, because he just left them sitting in the chariot. Today, the last of leaving Vrindavan: what Akrura sees in the water.
screen: `THE CHARIOT STOPS AT THE RIVER.` → `AKRURA DUCKS UNDER.` → `THE BOYS ARE IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Akrura does what anyone would do. He comes up for air and looks back at the bank. There's the chariot, and there are the two boys, sitting in it just as he left them. So he goes under again. And this time the vision is bigger. He sees Balarama as the great serpent Ananta, and resting on him, Vishnu himself, dark as a rain cloud, dressed in yellow, with sages and gods around him singing his praise. Akrura stays there in the river, and the Bhagavata gives him a long hymn of praise. Then he climbs out, dripping, and walks back to the chariot in a daze. Krishna looks at him and asks, kindly, whether he's seen something wonderful, in the earth or the sky or the water. And Akrura answers that every wonder in the earth, the sky and the water is in Krishna, and he's looking at him. So what does this scene do, here, on the road out of Vrindavan? The whole village has just watched Krishna leave. The gopis stood in the road until the dust was gone. And soon after, the text shows us a man discovering that the one he's driving to Mathura is also in the river, and also beyond all of it. The leaving is real; nobody in the story pretends it isn't. But the Bhagavata sets this vision right beside the grief, and some readers hear in it that the one who left the village hasn't left anything. Akrura gets back on the chariot, and they reach Mathura as the day ends. Krishna sends him on ahead, and walks into the city on foot, with the cowherds.
screen: `ON THE CHARIOT, AND IN THE RIVER.` · `VISHNU RESTING ON ANANTA.` · `EVERY WONDER IS IN YOU.` · then, large: `HE HASN'T LEFT ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and close your eyes, the way Akrura closed them before he went under. Let the breath be slow, like water. Now open your inner eyes to something ordinary you will see again today: a kitchen, a street, a face. Look at it in your mind as if you'd just come up from the river and found it still there. Nothing needs to change. Just look twice. If you pray, you can ask to see God, or Krishna, in what is right in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Leaving Vrindavan. The journey to Mathura, where Akrura sees the boys on the chariot, and also in the river, and Vishnu beyond them.
Your line: leaving Vrindavan. Today, before you decide you've seen all there is to something, go back and look again, the way Akrura went under twice. Day nine hundred four.

905.title: Kamsa's death
905.howItsDone: The story of Krishna in Mathura and Kamsa's end is recited from the Bhagavata and staged in Krishna plays and festivals in the region of Mathura and Vrindavan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of leaving Vrindavan: Akrura under the river, finding the boys there and in the chariot at once. What did you go back and look at again? Day nine hundred five.
screen: `LEAVING VRINDAVAN.` · `IN THE RIVER, AND IN THE CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: King Kamsa can't sleep. That afternoon, word reached the palace that a cowherd boy had walked into the festival hall and snapped the great bow on display, and fought off the guards. Now it's night, and everything Kamsa looks at seems wrong. The Bhagavata lists his omens. He looks at his reflection and can't see his head. He can't hear the sound of his own breath. He looks back for his footprints and finds none. The man who has spent the whole story hunting a child is now the one being hunted, by his own mind. Today and tomorrow, Kamsa's death.
screen: `THE GREAT BOW SNAPPED.` → `KAMSA CAN'T SLEEP.` → `NO HEAD IN THE REFLECTION.`

segments.voice: Morning comes, and with it the festival. Kamsa takes his seat on a high platform above the wrestling ground, ringed by his ministers and vassal kings. The citizens fill the stands. His champion wrestlers are ready. And at the gate, waiting for the boys, he's stationed a huge war elephant with orders to crush them. It doesn't work. Krishna fights the elephant, brings it down, and walks into the arena with one of its tusks on his shoulder, Balarama beside him. Then the Bhagavata stops the action and looks around the stands, one face at a time. To the wrestlers, Krishna looks like a thunderbolt. To the men of the city, the finest of men. To the women, love itself in a body. To the cowherds who came with him, their own kinsman. To unjust rulers, the one who will punish them. To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth. To his own clan, their deity. And to Kamsa, the text says, he looks like death. Same boy. Same moment. Same dusty arena. What each person sees depends on what each one brought in with them. The wrestlers came for a fight, and they see a weapon. His parents see their child. Kamsa brought a lifetime of fear, and fear is what walks in. Some readers take the scene as a teaching in a single picture: Krishna is met according to the heart that meets him. Tomorrow, the wrestling, and the end of the king who spent his life afraid.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT AT THE GATE.` · `A TUSK ON HIS SHOULDER.` · `ONE BOY, MANY EYES.` · then, large: `TO KAMSA, HE LOOKS LIKE DEATH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Bring to mind one person you'll see today. Notice what you're carrying toward them: an old irritation, a hope, a worry, a plan. Don't judge it. Just name what you're bringing in. Then, for a few breaths, try setting it down at the gate, and picture meeting them without it. Notice how they look then. If you pray, you can ask to meet God, or Krishna, without your armor on. The bell holds the time.
Kamsa's death. The end of the king of Mathura, who sees Krishna enter his arena and, the text says, sees death.
Your line: Kamsa's death. Today, before you walk into a room, ask yourself what you're bringing in with you. Day nine hundred five.

906.title: Kamsa's death
906.howItsDone: Kamsa's death and the freeing of Devaki and Vasudeva are retold from the Bhagavata, and Kamsa's defeat is acted out in festival performances in the Mathura area.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kamsa's death began: a sleepless king, an elephant at the gate, and one boy in the arena seen many ways, and by Kamsa, as death. What did you bring into a room yesterday? Day nine hundred six.

The women in the stands are not happy. Down on the wrestling ground, Kamsa's champion Chanura has squared off against Krishna, and his partner Mushtika against Balarama. Grown men built like mountains, against two boys from the cow pastures. The Bhagavata lets us hear the crowd: this is wrong, the women say to one another. It's no fair match. Whoever allowed it shares the blame. And they say the cowherd girls of Vraja were lucky, to see him every day. Today, the end of the fight, and the end of this part of the story.
screen: `CHANURA AND MUSHTIKA.` → `TWO BOYS AGAINST GIANTS.` → `THE CROWD SAYS, THIS IS WRONG.`

segments.voice: The fight goes hold for hold, and then it turns. Krishna brings down Chanura, Balarama brings down Mushtika, and the other wrestlers fall or run. The arena erupts. Kamsa, on his high platform, orders the music stopped. He shouts for the two boys to be driven out of the city, for the cowherds' goods to be seized and Nanda arrested, for Krishna's father Vasudeva and his own father Ugrasena to be killed. Before he finishes, Krishna is on the platform. Kamsa reaches for his sword. Krishna catches him by the hair, pulls him down into the arena, and it's over. Then the Bhagavata says something that's hard to forget. All his life, Kamsa thought of Krishna. Eating, drinking, walking, sleeping, he thought of nothing else, out of fear. And because his mind was so fixed on him, the text says, he reached him in the end. It's the same frame we heard at the rasa lila: what matters is where the mind is turned, even if it's turned there by terror. The story doesn't end only in triumph. Kamsa's wives come weeping, and Krishna comforts them and sees that the funeral rites are done. Then he goes to free his parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, whom Kamsa had put in chains again. He frees them and bows at their feet. And so this part closes where it began. The birth in a prison cell. The crossing of the Yamuna in the storm. Putana, the butter thief, the mouth full of the universe. Kaliya, Govardhan, the flute, the dance in the moonlight, the road out of Vrindavan. And now the cell door open, and a son kneeling in front of his mother.
screen: `THE WRESTLERS FALL.` · `HE WAS NEVER NOT THINKING OF HIM.` · `KAMSA'S WIVES ARE COMFORTED.` · then, large: `THE PRISON DOOR OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Kamsa spent his life running from what he feared, and the fear kept Krishna in his mind anyway. For these two minutes, bring to mind one small fear you've been carrying. Not the biggest one. Let it sit in front of you, and look at it plainly: its shape, its size, where you feel it in your body. Don't argue with it, and don't run. Breathe with it until it's simply there. Then, if you like, picture a door opening somewhere you've been shut in. If you pray, you can hold that fear before God, or before Krishna, for one breath. The bell holds the time.
Kamsa's death. The king who spent his life afraid of Krishna, pulled down in his own arena, and reaching him, the text says, through his fear.
Your line: Kamsa's death. Today, when an old fear comes back, look straight at it for one breath instead of running from it. Day nine hundred six.

907.title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
907.hook: a girl tries on the garland meant for the god
907.howItsDone: Andal is honored as one of the Alvars in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes; at Srivilliputtur, tradition holds that a garland worn by her image is still offered to the Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kamsa's death: the king whose fear kept his mind on Krishna all his life, pulled down in his own arena, and a prison door opening for Devaki and Vasudeva. What did your mind keep circling yesterday? Day nine hundred seven.

A garland of fresh flowers lies ready in a temple gardener's house, woven that morning for the image of Vishnu. While her father is out, his daughter picks it up. She puts it around her own neck. Then she leans over to see her reflection, and asks herself a question: would he want me? Except the he, for her, is the god the garland was made for. Today the path leaves the Bhagavata's village and meets the people who sang about it, starting in the Tamil south.
screen: `A GARLAND FOR THE GOD.` → `SHE TRIES IT ON FIRST.` → `WOULD HE WANT ME?`

segments.voice: The Alvars are the poet-saints of Vishnu who sang in Tamil. Tradition counts twelve of them, and explains the name as people who are immersed, sunk deep in God, the way you sink into water over your head. Their songs are not theology lectures. They are love songs, complaints, lullabies, longing. The girl with the garland is one of them. Her name is Andal. The story told about her goes like this. Her father, himself remembered as one of the Alvars, tends a flower garden for the temple. Tradition says he found her there as a baby, under a tulasi plant, and raised her as his own. She grows up on his stories of Krishna, and somewhere along the way she decides she will marry no one but the Lord. So she wears the garland before it goes to the temple. One day her father catches her. He's horrified: a garland someone has already worn can't be offered to God. He throws it out and weaves a new one. That night, the story says, the Lord comes to him in a dream and asks why the usual garland didn't arrive. The one she wore is the one he wants. From then on, her garlands go to the temple after she has worn them, and she gets a name for it: the girl who gave the garland she had worn. Sit with how strange that is. The rule of offering says fresh and untouched. And the story says God prefers the flowers that have already been warm against someone's neck, someone who loved him enough to try them on. The other name in today's title, Nammalvar, comes the day after tomorrow. Today it's enough to meet a gardener's daughter and a garland.
screen: `THE ALVARS: POETS SUNK DEEP IN GOD.` · `A BABY UNDER THE TULASI PLANT.` · `HER FATHER THROWS THE GARLAND OUT.` · `THE ONE SHE WORE IS THE ONE HE WANTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of something you give that isn't brand new: your tired attention at the end of a day, a meal you've made a hundred times, a phone call when you're half asleep. The kind of offering you might be tempted to throw out and redo. Hold it for a moment without fixing it. If you pray, you can offer it as it is, worn and warm, to God by whatever name you use. If you don't, simply notice that it was given. The bell holds the time.
The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu, whose name tradition explains as those sunk deep in God. Andal is the one who wore the garland first.
Your line: the Alvars, Andal and Nammalvar. Today, give one thing as it is, a little used and still warm, instead of waiting until it's perfect. Day nine hundred seven.

908.title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
908.hook: girls knocking on doors in the dark, waking each other up
908.howItsDone: During the Tamil month of Margazhi, Andal's Tiruppavai is sung before dawn in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes, and the day's verse is often recited in morning worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Alvars, and Andal, the gardener's daughter who wore the garland first, and the story where the Lord asked for the worn one. What did you give as it was, without redoing it? Day nine hundred eight.

It's still dark. Cold enough that nobody wants to leave the blanket. A group of girls is going from house to house, rapping on doors and calling through the windows to friends who are still asleep. Get up. The birds are already talking. You said you'd come. Are you deaf, or just pretending? One friend is teased for bragging yesterday that she'd be first awake. This is not a scene from a diary. It's a poem. Andal wrote it as a song cycle called the Tiruppavai, and today we walk with that group of girls.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, IN THE COLD.` → `KNOCKING ON FRIENDS' DOORS.` → `ANDAL'S TIRUPPAVAI.`

segments.voice: The Tiruppavai is set in the Tamil month of Margazhi, in the cold season. Andal imagines herself as one of the cowherd girls of Krishna's village, the same village we just left in the Bhagavata. The girls have taken a vow for the month: rise before dawn, bathe, keep simple, and go together to seek him. So the songs move like a morning. First they gather. Then they wake the girls who overslept, one door at a time, and it's affectionate and funny, the way friends really talk. Then they arrive at the house of Nanda, Krishna's foster father. They wake the doorkeeper. They wake Nanda, and Yashoda, and Krishna's brother. And at last they stand before Krishna himself and tell him why they've come. On the surface, they've come for a drum, a ritual drum for their vow. Then the songs turn. The drum was an excuse. What they want, they say, is to belong to him, to serve him, not just for today but in every life to come. Notice who is doing the seeking here. Not a lone hermit in a cave. A gang of friends, dragging each other out of bed, refusing to go without the one who's still asleep. In Andal's picture, nobody gets to the door alone, and nobody gets left behind for being lazy. They just knock louder. That's why these songs aren't only read. In Margazhi, people in Tamil homes and temples sing them before sunrise. A poem about getting up became a reason to get up.
screen: `THE COLD MONTH OF MARGAZHI.` · `WAKING THE GIRLS WHO OVERSLEPT.` · `AT NANDA'S DOOR.` · `NOT A DRUM, BUT TO BELONG TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the room be as quiet as an early morning. Bring to mind one person who has woken you up at some point in your life. Not with an alarm: someone who knocked, kept calling, wouldn't let you sleep through something that mattered. Let their face come clear. Then think of someone you might knock for. Just hold them in mind; you don't have to plan anything. If you pray, you can hold both of them before God in whatever words you already use. The bell holds the time.
The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Andal is the one who wrote the Tiruppavai, girls waking each other before dawn to go and find Krishna.
Your line: the Alvars, Andal and Nammalvar. Today, knock on one door: a message, a call, a nudge to someone you don't want to go without. Day nine hundred eight.

909.title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
909.hook: a silent boy under a tamarind tree, and a riddle that wakes him
909.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas recite Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temple worship and at home, and the tamarind tree at his temple town is honored as the place where he sat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Alvars again: Andal's Tiruppavai, girls knocking on doors before dawn so nobody went to Krishna alone. Whose door did you knock on? Day nine hundred nine.

A man is walking south, following a light. That's how the story tells it: he's far away in the north, on pilgrimage, and he sees a glow in the southern sky that no one else seems to notice. He follows it for a long way. It leads him to a temple town in the Tamil country, to a tamarind tree, and to a young man sitting in a hollow at its foot. Eyes closed. Not speaking. People there say he has been that way since he was a baby. The traveler has one question for him, and it's a riddle.
screen: `A LIGHT IN THE SOUTHERN SKY.` → `A TAMARIND TREE.` → `A YOUNG MAN WHO NEVER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: The young man is Nammalvar, the second name in our title. The traveler is Madhurakavi. Tradition says Nammalvar was born and didn't cry, didn't nurse, didn't open his eyes, and his worried parents left him at the temple, where he sat under the tamarind, silent, growing up in stillness. Madhurakavi wants to know whether anyone is home behind those closed eyes. So he asks, roughly: if a small thing is born inside something dead, what will it eat, and where will it lie? And for the first time, the story says, Nammalvar answers. It will eat that, and it will lie there. That's it. Two short lines, and Madhurakavi falls at his feet and becomes his disciple for life. What did they mean? Here traditional readers give more than one answer. One traditional reading: the small thing is the living self, born into a body that is, by itself, lifeless matter. Until it turns to God, it feeds on that body's pleasures and pains, and stays there. Other teachers take the riddle further, or differently. The tradition keeps the riddle and lets it stay a little open. Then the silent one starts to sing. The songs that follow, gathered as the Tiruvaymoli, are full of longing for Vishnu. In some, he speaks as a girl pining for her absent lover, and her mother and friends speak about her. Sri Vaishnava tradition holds these songs so high it calls them the Tamil Veda. And Madhurakavi? He is remembered among the Alvars too, for a short poem in praise of no one but his teacher. A man who walked a long way after a light, and found it sitting very still.
screen: `A CHILD WHO NEVER CRIED.` · `THE RIDDLE: WHAT WILL IT EAT?` · `IT WILL EAT THAT, AND LIE THERE.` · `THE SILENT ONE BEGINS TO SING.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes close, or rest them low, like the young man under the tree. Sit still enough that your body gets quiet. Then turn the riddle over gently, without needing to solve it. Something small and alive, inside something that would be still without it. Feel the breath moving in a body that sits motionless. Don't push for an answer. Just let the question sit with you, the way Madhurakavi's question sat in the silence before it was answered. If you pray, you can rest in God's presence in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Nammalvar is the silent one under the tamarind, who answered a riddle and then sang the Tiruvaymoli.
Your line: the Alvars, Andal and Nammalvar. Today, before you answer one question, let it sit in silence for a breath. Day nine hundred nine.

910.title: the Nayanars
910.hook: a hunter who worships Shiva all wrong, and all right
910.howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus in Tamil Nadu honor the Nayanars in temples, often with images of them in a row, and Kannappa is especially remembered at the Shiva temple of Srikalahasti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Alvars once more: Nammalvar, silent under the tamarind, answering a riddle in two short lines before he began to sing. Did you let a question sit before you answered? Day nine hundred ten.
screen: `THE ALVARS.` · `IT WILL EAT THAT, AND LIE THERE.`

segments.voice: Every morning a priest climbs a hill to a small shrine of Shiva, and every morning he finds a mess. Bits of meat on the stone. Flowers that look like they've been stuck in somebody's hair. Water splashed everywhere, as if someone spat it. He cleans it all, does the worship properly, and goes home upset. The next morning, the same. Someone is worshiping here, and doing it all wrong. Today the path crosses from the poet-saints of Vishnu to the poet-saints of Shiva, and starts with the person making the mess.
screen: `A MESS AT SHIVA'S SHRINE.` → `EVERY MORNING, THE SAME.` → `WHO IS DOING THIS?`

segments.voice: The Nayanars are the Tamil saints of Shiva. Tradition counts sixty-three of them, and their lives are told in a long Tamil work, the Periya Puranam. They're a mixed crowd: kings and housewives, a potter, a washerman, a hunter. Today's is the hunter, Tinnan. Out tracking in the hills, he comes across the shrine and something in him simply breaks open. He has no idea how worship is done. So he does what a hunter would do for someone he loves. He carries water in his mouth, because he has no pot. He brings flowers tucked in his hair, because his hands are full with his bow. And he brings meat he has roasted and tasted first, to make sure only the best goes to Shiva. That's the mess. In the story, Shiva tells the priest in a dream to hide and watch. So the priest is crouched behind the shrine the day the image's eye starts to bleed. Tinnan tries herbs. Nothing. So he takes an arrow, digs out his own eye, and presses it into place. The bleeding stops. Then the other eye of the image starts to bleed. Tinnan sets his foot on the spot, so he can find it once he's blind, and lifts the arrow to his second eye. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and stops him. From then on, the story says, he's called Kannappa, a name that's tied to his eye. Look back over this week and there's a thread. Krishna's village loved him without any rulebook. Andal wore the garland first. Now a hunter tastes the meat first. Again and again, the stories let love break the rule of the untouched offering, and the priest who knows every rule is the one sent to watch.
screen: `THE NAYANARS: SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `WATER IN HIS MOUTH, MEAT TASTED FIRST.` · `HIS OWN EYE FOR THE BLEEDING ONE.` · `SHIVA'S HAND STOPS HIM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let your hands rest open. Think of the clumsiest way you've ever shown love. A burnt meal. A gift that missed. Words that came out wrong. Don't wince at it; look at it the way the story looks at Tinnan, from behind the shrine, seeing what he was actually trying to give. Then breathe out, and let it be enough. If you pray, you can offer whatever you have today, clumsy as it is, to God by any name you already use. The bell holds the time.
The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva, whose lives the Periya Puranam tells. Kannappa is the hunter who offered his own eye.
